issues.item: Escape Route Planning: always plan an escape route before entering a place
issues.explanation: Escape route planning implies a prominent ongoing external-danger/triggered-threat pattern in public places, but the formulation specifies no active links involving Triggers or Threat, and the rest of the profile is centered on bodily vulnerability and negative beliefs rather than situational danger. This makes the item poorly aligned with the formulation and cross-node content.

issues.item: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem
issues.explanation: Distrust of others is not impossible after a life-threatening accident, but in this profile it introduces an interpersonal/paranoid theme that is not supported by the other selected items or the formulation. The remaining items focus on bodily unreliability and permanent damage after an accident, so this item is the least coherent with the trauma-linked appraisal pattern presented.

vignette:
Amir al-Rashid is a seventy-five-year-old sculptor who came to see me three months after a life-threatening accident in his studio. He is a widower of eight years, a father of two grown daughters, and has lived alone in the same house in Dearborn, Michigan, since his wife passed. For forty years, he has worked in bronze and stone, shaping figures that seemed to emerge from the material rather than being imposed upon it. That work stopped the day a six-hundred-pound block of marble, suspended from a chain hoist, slipped its cradle and crashed onto the hydraulic lift table where he had been standing moments earlier. The impact threw him backward against a steel shelving unit; he struck his head and lost consciousness for an unknown period. When he came to, he was on the floor, the marble block resting at an angle against the table’s leg, his left arm pinned beneath a fallen chisel stand. He could not move his legs for what felt like an eternity, though in truth it was only until the paramedics arrived. He was hospitalized for three days with a concussion, three fractured ribs, and a deep contusion across his lower back. The doctors told him he was lucky; the block had missed his spine by inches.

Amir does not feel lucky. What he feels, most days, is that his body has become something foreign and untrustworthy, a vessel that can no longer be relied upon to carry him safely through the world. He has come to believe that the accident did not just bruise his ribs but permanently altered him, that he is now a person who is fundamentally damaged and who will never return to who he was before. This belief is not abstract. It lives in the way he moves through his house now, one hand always touching the wall, his eyes scanning the floor for obstacles that were never there before. He checks his body constantly—his pulse, his breathing, the sensation in his legs, the tightness in his chest—searching for evidence that something is going wrong, that another catastrophe is imminent. Every twinge, every ache, every moment of dizziness becomes a confirmation: his body is failing him, and he must remain vigilant.

The studio, once the center of his life, is now sealed. He has not entered it since the day of the accident. The chain hoist hangs motionless; the marble block has been removed by the fire department, but the space still holds the violence of that moment. Amir tells me he cannot bear to look at it. He avoids any situation that puts his body under physical stress—lifting, climbing, even walking on uneven ground. He has stopped going to the grocery store because the parking lot is sloped and he fears slipping. His daughter brings him food twice a week. He has stopped attending Friday prayers at the mosque because the walk from the car to the entrance involves three steps, and he is certain he will misjudge them and fall. He knows this sounds unreasonable, and he says so, but the fear does not yield to reason. It is a felt certainty, lodged somewhere deeper than thought.

In the evenings, he sits in his armchair and finds himself thinking, over and over, about why this happened to him. He was careful. He had checked the hoist that morning. He had done everything right. The question circles back without answer: why him, why now, why did he survive when the marble could have crushed him? He does not frame this as searching for meaning in any spiritual sense. It is more like a wound he keeps pressing, a loop of rumination that offers no relief but which he cannot stop. He is tired. He is lonely. He is afraid that he will never work again, and that without his work, he does not know who he is.

What brought him to my office was a phone call from his younger daughter, Layla, who lives in Chicago. She told him she could hear the fear in his voice. She told him she was worried. He came because he did not want to be a burden, because he could see that his avoidance had already reshaped his life into something small and narrow. He is afraid of what he might find in therapy—afraid that talking about the accident will bring it back, that he will relive the moment he could not move his legs, that he will discover the damage is permanent in ways even he has not yet admitted. But he is also afraid of staying the same. He told me, in our first session, that he had always believed a sculptor’s job was to reveal what was already inside the stone. He wondered, quietly, whether something inside him was still waiting to be revealed, or whether the stone had finally won.
